newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin honours ally, music great Rostropovich.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin honours ally, music great Rostropovich.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin awarded cellist Mstislav Rostropovich the order "for services to the fatherland" on Wednesday, as much in recognition of his political support for the Russian president as for his contribution to world music.
Yeltsin said he was "proud that Russia has given the world this great musician and great man".
Rostropovich, in Russia as part of a 70th birthday tour, was stripped of his citizenship by the Soviet authorities in 1978 and only rehabilitated by president Mikhail Gorbachev in 1990.
He flew in haste to Moscow in August 1991 to join Yeltsin's resistance to a hardline communist coup attempt and has since been a prominent campaigner for democratic reform.
Rostropovich spent his actual birthday on March 27 in Paris, his second home, surrounded by European royalty and political and business leaders at a glittering charity concert.
He said he chose to mark the day there because he could not accept a lavish proposed state-funded celebration in Russia while his countrymen were in dire financial straits.
But on Tuesday evening he was greeted with thunderous applause from the audience at the Moscow Conservatory, his old school, where he accepted a new state award for music.
"Rostropovich's life has inspired the greatest composers of the 20th century," Yeltsin was quoted as saying by Itar-Tass news agency. He underlined the musician's contribution to defending democracy.
Tass said Rostropovich was clearly moved by the Kremlin meeting with Yeltsin. The order "for services to the fatherland" first class, is one of the highest awards Russia can bestow.
"Throughout my 70 years of life I have dreamed of a free Russia, about its happy future...I believe that it will be so," the agency quoted the cellist as saying.
"I am happy to see my friend Boris Yeltsin full of strength and energy," said Rostropovich, who tired out the bodyguard assigned to him by Yeltsin during the short-lived coup attempt.

Rostropovich, who travels between the United States, France and Russia and is also a brilliant conductor and pianist, is regarded by music critics as still being at the height of his performing powers at an age when most people have retired.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Rostropovich said he was impressed by post-Soviet Moscow, which he said was becoming more and more like a European capital.

But he bemoaned the spread of rock music among Russia's youth: "Even now we have wonderful performers who do not express their emotion by the decibel level. But on the whole I see a lack of taste on television, crude texts and absolutely pathetic musical expression."
The Kremlin ceremony was attended by members of Yeltsin and Rostropovich's families and by leading cultural figures.

First deputy prime ministers Boris Nemstov and Anatoly Chubais were summoned by Yeltsin for the ceremony from parliament. They were supposed to stay and answer questions from the lower house, which is dominated by communists and their allies.
